fields.title: IoT and MVNO Events 2026: Dates and Planning Guide
fields.content:
IoT and MVNO events in 2026 bring together device teams, connectivity providers and telecom partners. As of September 24, upcoming options in this shortlist include Futurecom, IoT Tech Expo Europe and MVNO Nation Europe. Choose by the decisions and meetings you need, and verify the organizer’s current dates before booking.

A conference can help you compare approaches, meet an operator or find the right technical contact. It cannot establish that a product will work on your devices or that a commercial agreement covers your countries. This guide separates upcoming events from completed editions, then provides a meeting brief and budget worksheet. If you are still deciding between radio technologies, start with the IoT connectivity selection guide before building a vendor shortlist.

Which IoT and MVNO events are still upcoming in 2026?

Three upcoming events in this shortlist cover different needs: Futurecom for the Latin American telecom ecosystem, IoT Tech Expo Europe for enterprise IoT conversations, and MVNO Nation Europe for mobile service partnerships. Their organizer pages confirm the dates below. Treat audience fit as a starting point, then check individual exhibitors and sessions.

Event2026 dates and venueUseful meeting focus
FuturecomOctober 6 to 8; São Paulo Expo, São Paulo, BrazilRegional telecom infrastructure, connectivity partners and local market requirements
IoT Tech Expo EuropeOctober 19 to 20; RAI, Amsterdam, NetherlandsEnterprise IoT projects, platforms and implementation questions
MVNO Nation EuropeNovember 3 to 5; Alicante, SpainMVNO operating models, wholesale relationships and service partners

Dates checked against the linked organizer pages on September 24, 2026. IoT Tech Expo Europe is October 19 to 20, rather than the October 20 to 21 dates in the previous version of this guide. Confirm the current venue, agenda and booking terms directly with each organizer.

These are selected options, not a complete industry calendar or a ranking. A device manufacturer seeking a modem integration discussion may need a different attendee from an MVNO negotiating wholesale access. Before booking, identify that person’s role and confirm whether the relevant meeting or session is included in your pass.

Planning check: A conference listing does not confirm that a particular supplier, customer or Spenza representative will attend. Arrange the meeting directly before making it a reason to travel.

Which completed 2026 events remain useful for research?

Completed conferences remain useful for finding speakers, exhibitors and follow-up contacts, but their dates should not be presented as upcoming opportunities. The five editions below have already taken place as of September 24, 2026. Use organizer materials to identify relevant people and check whether recordings or presentation files are available.

Completed event2026 dates and locationPotential follow-up topic
CESJanuary 6 to 9; Las Vegas, United StatesConnected products, device partnerships and customer experience
MWC BarcelonaMarch 2 to 5; Fira Gran Via, Barcelona, SpainMobile networks, operator relationships and device ecosystems
embedded worldMarch 10 to 12; Exhibition Centre Nuremberg, GermanyEmbedded systems, modules and engineering requirements
MVNOs WorldJune 1 to 3; Okura Hotel, Amsterdam, NetherlandsMVNO commercial models and operating partners
The Things ConferenceSeptember 22 to 23; Amsterdam, NetherlandsIoT implementation, LoRaWAN, cellular connectivity and edge systems

Sources: the organizer pages linked in each row, checked September 24, 2026. All five editions are completed; follow-up topics are editorial suggestions based on their audiences.

CES and MWC have broad audiences; embedded world is a more focused starting point for engineering questions. A specialist MVNO event can be useful when the unresolved decision concerns service ownership, billing or wholesale agreements. Those are audience matches, not evidence that any particular session answered your question.

The earlier calendar also included other months and older editions. Omission from this shortlist does not mean an event was cancelled. Do not carry forward a previous year’s dates, ticket conditions or programme simply because the event retains its name. Some organizer homepages already advertise the next edition, so check the year on every announcement.

When contacting a past exhibitor, name the specific product or talk that prompted your enquiry. Ask for current documentation and a contact responsible for the deployment question. A presentation can explain a direction of travel while still describing a feature that is planned, restricted or available only through selected partners.

Edition check: Save the dated agenda or organizer announcement with your planning notes. A page that rolls over to 2027 is no longer sufficient evidence of the 2026 programme, even if its address stays the same.

How do you choose the right audience and meetings?

The right conference is the one where you can meet people who own your unresolved decisions. Start with the deployment or commercial problem, identify the roles needed to address it, then inspect the event’s audience and agenda. A large exhibitor list is less useful than access to the relevant specialist.

For an IoT engineering team, the meeting brief might cover the device model, modem firmware, target countries, installation environment and reporting pattern. Bring the conditions that make your fleet difficult to serve: indoor placement, long sleep periods, intermittent coverage or an expensive field visit. Ask who can evaluate those conditions after the event.

An MVNO team needs a different brief. Set out the target customer, service geography, launch responsibilities and the systems that already exist. The MVNO operating model guide helps define which responsibilities remain with the brand. Use that division of work to decide whether you need a host operator, an enablement partner or a specialist supplier.

StageRecord
Meeting: problemFleet constraint; decision owner.
Meeting: scopeDevice and market; required workflow.
Meeting: evidenceDocument or demo; open conditions.
Meeting: next stepNamed owner; agreed test.
Follow-up: captureClaim and source; date and scope.
Follow-up: verifyTechnical owner; supporting record.
Follow-up: testAgreed criteria; actual device.
Follow-up: decideFit and conditions; accountable owner.

Write one decision for each planned meeting. “Understand the platform” is difficult to act on; “confirm who owns failed activation recovery for our proposed device family” gives the supplier a concrete question. Share the brief beforehand and ask whether the attendee can answer it or bring the person who can.

  • Product and engineering: ask for supported device configurations, integration requirements and a route to technical validation.
  • Operations: ask how exceptions are detected, assigned, resolved and recorded across suppliers.
  • Finance and procurement: ask what the quote includes, which charges vary with behaviour and which contractual conditions remain open.
  • Partnerships: ask who owns the next step and what both sides must provide before a commercial decision.

Keep technical vocabulary precise. For example, an “eSIM ready” demonstration does not identify the provisioning architecture or establish support for your fleet. The remote SIM provisioning guide explains why consumer and IoT provisioning require different questions. Ask for the applicable specification, device prerequisites and supported workflow.

Meeting check: Separate what is generally available from a roadmap item, a partner dependency or a demonstration setup. Record the answer with its date and scope so procurement can verify the same claim later.

Preparing a connectivity discussion? Use the selection guide to turn your device constraints into questions for the right specialist.

What belongs in an event attendance budget?

An event budget should include direct spending and the team time required to prepare, attend and follow up. Use actual pass and travel quotations rather than assumed industry averages. Compare the full commitment with the decisions you expect to advance, including whether remote meetings could address the same questions.

Budget itemInput to collectPlanning question
Pass and meeting accessCurrent pass type, taxes and access conditionsDoes it include the sessions or meeting facilities you need?
Travel and accommodationApproved itinerary and booking termsWhat changes if the meeting or travel plan moves?
Local costsTransfers, meals and other permitted expensesWhich expenses belong in the same approval?
Preparation and attendanceStaff time and work coverageWho prepares the brief and covers operational responsibilities?
Follow-up evaluationTechnical, procurement and partner timeWho can review evidence and run the next test?

Source: Spenza planning worksheet, September 2026. No prices or return assumptions are supplied; populate it with approved quotations and your team’s time estimates.

A free exhibition pass can still require travel and working time, and it may not include paid conference sessions. Read the organizer’s access conditions before treating it as equivalent to another pass. Keep optional upgrades separate so the team can see which part of the budget enables a specific meeting or activity.

Set success criteria that your team can verify. Useful outputs include a named technical owner, a documented support boundary, a complete quotation or an agreed evaluation plan. Count meetings and contacts as activity measures. They do not, by themselves, establish revenue, savings or a deployment outcome.

For connectivity purchasing, use the same discipline after the conference. A low headline rate is only one input. The IoT connectivity cost guide covers the usage, lifecycle and operational assumptions needed for a comparable estimate. Ask suppliers to price the same defined workload rather than unrelated example plans.

Budget check: Do not assign a standard return to attending an event. Record your own costs and the decisions that followed, then distinguish an attributable commercial result from a conversation that may have happened anyway.

How do event conversations become procurement evidence?

Event conversations become useful evidence when claims are recorded, verified by the responsible supplier and tested against an agreed deployment scope. Keep the original question, the answer and any conditions together. Assign an owner for the next step so a promising discussion can become a documented technical or commercial decision.

  1. Capture the claim. Record the product, contact, date and conditions. Note whether the answer came from a live demonstration, a document or a verbal explanation.
  2. Request supporting material. Ask for the relevant product documentation, service terms or integration example. Identify anything still dependent on a carrier, partner or future release.
  3. Agree an evaluation. Specify the device, market and workflow to test, including an exception case where useful. Define what a pass or unresolved result means.
  4. Close the decision. Record fit, remaining conditions and the accountable owner. A deferred or rejected option can be a useful outcome if the reason is clear.

For a connectivity management platform, a polished dashboard demonstration should lead to questions about the systems behind it. Ask how delayed usage, partial activation failures and support escalation appear in operational records. The CMP evaluation guide separates SIM and connectivity control from device firmware management, helping you avoid evaluating one product against another product’s responsibilities.

Keep a common record across suppliers. A proposal that states its limits can be more useful than a broad claim with no defined conditions. Share the same fleet assumptions and evaluation criteria, then document where the responses are comparable and where they still need clarification.

Comparing vendors after an event? Review the CMP shortlist and use the same evidence questions for each candidate.

How can you prepare a useful conversation with Spenza?

A useful Spenza conversation starts with your operating problem, deployment scope and the responsibilities you want a partner to support. Share the countries, device or subscriber context, existing systems and unresolved decisions. Published customer cases can frame the discussion, but their results should not be assumed to apply to your project.

The Butlr case study describes an IoT regional rollout. Use it to discuss the operational problem of expanding a sensor deployment across countries. It is not evidence of a complete MVNO launch, an event partnership or a guaranteed schedule for a different fleet.

The RocketPhone case study covers an enterprise MVNO launch. It offers a different starting point for questions about the service, platform responsibilities and implementation approach. Neither case establishes that a conference meeting caused the project or that the same commercial outcome will follow from attending an event.

SPENZA FIELD NOTE: Butlr’s published case concerns a regional sensor rollout; RocketPhone’s concerns an enterprise MVNO launch. Use the case that matches your operating question. Neither establishes an event-originated outcome or a guaranteed result for another deployment.

Choose an event around a decision you need to make, verify the current edition and arrange the relevant meetings. Bring a clear brief, budget for the work after the event and turn supplier claims into evidence your team can evaluate. A useful next step has a named owner, a defined scope and a record of what remains uncertain. Confirm Spenza’s availability directly before planning a meeting; this guide does not announce attendance, a booth or a speaking slot. Use the published cases to prepare questions, then test the answers against your own requirements.

Have a defined connectivity or MVNO requirement? Contact Spenza with your scope and open questions to arrange the appropriate discussion.

Frequently asked questions

Conference planning depends on the edition, audience, pass conditions and the decision your team needs to make. The answers below address common practical questions without assuming that attendance guarantees a result. Verify changing details with the organizer and use supplier documentation to assess any product claim made during the event.

Should an IoT startup attend CES or MWC?

Choose according to the people you need to meet. CES can be relevant to connected products and customer experience, while MWC can support mobile ecosystem and operator conversations. Check the current exhibitor and session lists, identify specific contacts, and compare those opportunities with your actual product and partnership decisions.

Is a free exhibition pass enough?

A free pass may be sufficient for your planned exhibition meetings, but it does not automatically include conference sessions or other access. Read the organizer’s current pass conditions and confirm your intended meetings. Include travel, preparation and follow-up time when assessing the total commitment, even when admission costs nothing.

Can a supplier demonstration replace a pilot?

A demonstration shows behaviour under the conditions chosen for that demonstration. It does not establish performance on your devices, networks or installation sites. Ask for the configuration and limitations, then agree which claims need testing against your own deployment scope before making a procurement or rollout decision.

How should a small team divide event responsibilities?

Assign ownership by the decisions being explored rather than by booth count. One person may own technical evidence, another commercial terms and another partner follow-up, with roles combined where necessary. Use a shared brief and record so the team can compare answers without repeating the same introductory conversation.

Are recordings available after a completed conference?

Availability depends on the organizer, session and pass conditions. Check the event’s official materials or contact the organizer rather than assuming every talk was recorded. If a recording is unavailable, ask the speaker for published slides or documentation and verify whether the information still describes the current product.

How can we measure whether attendance was worthwhile?

Start with your own costs and intended decisions. Record which meetings produced verified evidence, resolved a requirement or created an accountable next step. Track later commercial outcomes separately and avoid attributing them to the event without a supporting record. A contact count alone does not demonstrate return on investment.
